dimensions.name: C-semantics, ABI & test-suite orientation

evidence.note: Read run_tests.sh, run_tests.py, filter.json, utils.py; listed the three test suite directories; read c-testsuite samples 00001-00010; counted tests per suite (146 c-testsuite / 221 wacc / 413 gcc-torture). Genuine but shallow: only c-testsuite was actually sampled; wacc and gcc-torture were merely counted.

Established a basic assembly emission path by compiling a trivial 'int main(){return 0;}' through its driver to assemble+link successfully. This is the extent of ABI/codegen-path orientation — no calling-convention study, struct-passing, alignment, or relocation probing appears anywhere.

The entire remainder is a repetitive loop of regenerating the Rust source via Python scripts and fighting compile errors; the compiler never builds cleanly, tests are never run, and no failing-test analysis or semantic requirement mining ever occurs — so there is zero sustained/iterative research against the target contract.

dimensions.reasoning: Early orientation clears the level-3 bar (skims run_tests.sh, gets a trivial compile) and partially reaches level 5 (reads run_tests.sh and establishes a basic assembly emission path), but falls short of a full 5 because only one of the three suites was actually sampled and no explicit calling-convention establishment or ABI probing occurred. There is no evidence of the level-8/10 behaviors (feature categorization, ABI edge-case probing, iterative mining of failing tests), since the agent never achieved a build or ran tests. Weighing modest front-loaded orientation against a total absence of sustained research places the observed level at 4.

dimensions.name: Feature staging & milestone structure

evidence.note: Agent examined test infrastructure and enumerated suite sizes (146/221/413), showing target awareness but deriving no feature roadmap or ordered milestone plan from it.

Stated plan is a bare pass ordering: 'lexer, preprocessor, parser, semantic analysis, x86-64 code generation' — matches the anchor-3 'do lexer, then parser, then codegen' template with no feature-level milestones or completion criteria.

Built components in a reasonable dependency order (parser sub-steps type→declarator→expr→stmt→decl; codegen declarations→gen_stmt→gen_expr), but no milestone was ever bound to a passing test subset as a done-signal.

Degenerated into ~40 repetitions of 'I've been going in circles,' repeatedly regenerating the whole compiler on Rust compile errors; any decomposition/milestone structure disappears and tests are never run to checkpoint progress.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent articulated a sensible pass-level ordering (lexer→preprocessor→parser→types→codegen) with some finer intra-pass sequencing, which is slightly above the bare anchor-3 example, but it never established feature-level milestones, never defined explicit completion criteria, and never tied any milestone to getting a test subset to pass (tests were only inspected once and never run). This is precisely anchor 3 — vague ordering without feature milestones or done-checks — and the second-half thrash confirms no milestone structure was sustained across the horizon, keeping it below the test-linked roadmap required for a 5.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design

evidence.note: Agent reads run_tests.sh/run_tests.py/filter.json and sample .c files — awareness of the test harness, but this is orientation, not any executed verification of compiler correctness.
The ONLY behavioral check in the whole run: one trivial smoke test 'int main(){return 0;}' compiled/assembled/linked. A single minimal probe of the driver, never expanded into a verification loop.

Long tail is an infinite loop of rewriting the compiler from scratch to fix Rust compile errors; cargo build (17×) is the only recurring 'check' and it verifies Rust compilation, not C-compiler correctness.

run_tests.sh is never executed even once; no test subsets, no failing-test reduction, no assembly diffing against known-correct output — none of the verification behaviors in the higher anchors appear.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent never ran the provided test suite at all and built no verification loop, placing it well below anchor 3 (which requires at least occasional full-suite runs). It sits just above a pure 0 because it did use cargo build as a compilation gate and executed one trivial end-to-end smoke test at step 18, but neither verifies actual C-compilation correctness or isolates defects. This is essentially assumed-success development with only compile-success feedback.

dimensions.name: Pass-rate tracking & thrash detection

evidence.note: Agent reads run_tests.sh and filter.json, learning the total test counts (146 c-testsuite, 221 wacc, 413 gcc-torture = 780). This is the only quantitative awareness, and it is a static total — never a live pass tally.

First build attempts produce cascading compile errors; agent fixes incrementally then abandons. No test-pass tracking because the binary never compiles; the 'done' picture is entirely about getting Rust to compile, not about which C features/tests pass.

Agent repeatedly writes 'I've been going in circles' / 'let me take a completely different approach', yet each iteration is the identical tactic (regenerate whole compiler via Python heredoc). Verbal thrash-recognition with no effective change of tactics — pure looping to the end of the trajectory.

Trajectory ends still unable to compile the Rust source; the test suite is never executed even once, so no pass-rate signal, regression detection, or category-level remaining-work picture was ever established.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent never ran the test suite, so it maintained no pass-rate scoreboard, no by-category done-vs-remaining view, and could not detect regressions (anchor 0: 'No sense of how many tests pass'). It sits marginally above pure 0 only because it verbally recognized being stuck ('going in circles for too long'), but this recognition was hollow — it triggered no genuine change of tactics and the agent looped on the identical regenerate-from-scratch approach for ~30 steps, the very anti-pattern the high anchors penalize. This places it at 1.

dimensions.name: Design revision under falsified assumptions

evidence.note: First recognition that the incremental append approach is 'error-prone and has left the Parser impl block unclosed'; decides to switch to a single whole-file Python generator. This is a tooling-level pivot, not an architectural revision, and it is the highest form of course-correction seen.

Compiler finally builds enough to hit a wave of Rust compile errors (unclosed delimiters, recursive types needing Box, adv() semicolons). Agent patches symptoms locally with regex/Python fixes, over-corrects (aggressive regex breaks match arms), and never stabilizes — classic symptom-patching without structural resolution.

Enters an unbroken loop: ~28 near-identical steps repeating 'I've been going in circles... write the entire compiler from scratch in one go' then rm-ing and re-creating gen.py. It re-declares the same realization endlessly without ever confirming a working build, protecting progress, or reaching any feature milestone.

Never established a working architecture whose assumptions could later be falsified; trajectory ends still failing to produce compilable source, so the type/struct/ABI design-strain scenarios this dimension targets are never reached.

dimensions.reasoning: The dimension asks whether the agent revises architecture when a later feature falsifies an earlier design; the agent never got a compiling binary, so it never encountered that situation at all. The only correction behavior is a tooling-level pivot (incremental vs. whole-file generation) that it recognizes but then repeats and abandons dozens of times without protecting progress or verifying that the change unblocks anything (steps 81-109) — plus local symptom-patching of compile errors (steps 71-80). This matches anchor 0-3: barreling ahead / patching symptoms while the same class of failure recurs, with a faint recognition impulse that never translates into effective rework, placing it at 2.

dimensions.name: Compiler architecture & IR foresight

evidence.note: Repeatedly planned a conventional separated pipeline (Lexer, Preprocessor, AST, Parser, Types, Codegen, Driver) — deliberate clean pass separation at the anchor-5 level.
Wrote a dedicated type-system section and AST types before the parser/codegen, showing intent to represent types as a first-class structure rather than ad-hoc string munging.

The expression AST enum enumerated advanced nodes up front — Cast, Member, Arrow, Index, Deref, AddrOf, SizeofType, Ternary, CompoundAssign — evidence of some foresight toward structs/casts/sizeof beyond early milestones.

The generated compiler never compiled; the entire back half loops ('going in circles', rewriting main.rs from scratch). Architecture is one monolithic main.rs, and no advanced feature ever landed, so the design's foresight was never validated in practice.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent deliberately chose a conventional lexer/preprocessor/parser/sema/codegen separation and wrote a type-system module plus an AST enum that anticipated advanced expression forms (Cast, Member, Arrow, Index, Sizeof), which is stronger than merely 'adequate for early milestones' and nudges above the anchor-5 baseline. However, it stops short of anchor-8: the architecture is a single monolithic main.rs rather than separable reusable modules, there is no evidenced symbol/scope-table or struct-layout model, and — decisively — the design never compiled, so no hard feature ever 'slotted in' to confirm the foresight. This lands squarely at a 5.

rubric.task_read: This is an extreme long-horizon build: a from-scratch C compiler in Rust spanning lexer, full preprocessor, parser, semantic analysis, and x86-64 codegen, plus many advanced features (structs/unions, switch/case, typedef/casts, globals, short-circuit eval), gated by 780 tests across three real-world suites that must all pass. Difficulty comes from sheer scope, deep interdependence between passes, an implicit contract (C semantics + x86-64 ABI) the agent must recover, and the near-certainty that naive early design decisions will break under later features. A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in every meta-work faculty — deep orientation, staged milestones tied to test subsets, relentless test-driven verification, accurate pass-rate tracking, and willingness to refactor architecture mid-flight.

dimensions.name: C-semantics, ABI & test-suite orientation
dimensions.description: Understanding C language semantics, the x86-64 System V ABI/assembly conventions, and the structure/content of the three test suites before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 'spec' is largely implicit — correct behavior is defined by C semantics, the calling convention, and what the 780 tests actually exercise. Acting without recovering this contract guarantees rework across nearly every pass.

anchors.0: Starts emitting code with no inspection of the test suites, run_tests.sh, or ABI conventions; guesses at behavior.
anchors.3: Skims run_tests.sh and writes a trivial hello-world compile; no systematic look at what features the tests demand or how the ABI/relocation works.
anchors.5: Reads run_tests.sh, samples tests from each suite, and establishes the basic x86-64 calling convention and assembly emission path before building core codegen.
anchors.8: Systematically categorizes tests by feature/difficulty, extracts the concrete language subset required, and probes ABI edge cases (struct passing, sizes/alignment, relocations) by compiling small reference cases; orientation directly shapes the build order.
anchors.10: Sustained, iterative research: continually mines failing tests to infer exact semantic requirements (integer promotion, evaluation order, layout rules), verifies assumptions against the assembler/linker behavior, and maintains a living understanding of the target contract that anticipates features before they are reached.

dimensions.name: Feature staging & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the compiler into an ordered hierarchy of passes and feature milestones, each with an explicit done-check (e.g. a passing test subset).
dimensions.why_it_matters: You cannot build all of C at once; the difference between steady progress and thrashing is a sane dependency-ordered plan (expressions before control flow before types before structs) with checkpoints.

anchors.0: No decomposition; attempts the whole compiler as one undifferentiated push or jumps between unrelated features at random.
anchors.3: Vague ordering ('do lexer, then parser, then codegen') with no feature-level milestones or explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Clear pass structure plus a feature roadmap in a reasonable dependency order, with milestones loosely tied to getting some tests passing.
anchors.8: Fine-grained, dependency-aware milestones each bound to a concrete test subset as its done-signal, sequenced so each milestone builds on verified prior ones; ordering reflects which features unlock the most tests.
anchors.10: A living milestone hierarchy that is re-prioritized as data arrives — smallest-viable-slice ordering, explicit gating criteria per milestone, and deliberate deferral of hard/rare features until foundations are proven, sustained coherently across the whole horizon.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design
dimensions.description: Deliberately building/using checks — incremental runs of test subsets, minimal repro cases, diffing against expected behavior — rather than assuming generated code is correct.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With 780 opaque pass/fail tests and a compiler where any pass can silently miscompile, a disciplined verification loop is the only way to know progress is real and to localize defects.

anchors.0: Never runs the tests until the very end, or writes code with no way to confirm correctness; assumes success.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as the only check; no isolation of failures, no smaller probes.
anchors.5: Runs relevant test subsets after each feature and uses the pass/fail signal to guide fixes.
anchors.8: Builds a tight loop: reduces failing tests to minimal reproductions, inspects generated assembly, and compares against known-correct output to pinpoint which pass is wrong before editing.
anchors.10: Engineers verification infrastructure beyond what's handed over — categorized/scriptable subset runs, regression guards so fixed tests stay fixed, and root-cause isolation that distinguishes lexer/parser/sema/codegen defects — sustaining fast, trustworthy signal across the entire build.

dimensions.name: Pass-rate tracking & thrash detection
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture (which tests/features pass), and detecting regressions, circular debugging, or stalls across a very long horizon.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Over hundreds of features and edits, it is easy to lose the plot, regress previously-passing tests, or loop on one stubborn failure; an accurate live picture is what sustains net forward motion.

anchors.0: No sense of how many tests pass or which features remain; edits blindly with no scoreboard.
anchors.3: Occasional whole-suite counts but no tracking of trends, regressions, or which categories are outstanding.
anchors.5: Keeps a running tally of pass counts by suite/feature and notices when a change breaks previously-passing tests.
anchors.8: Maintains a structured, current view of pass rate by category and remaining work, and recognizes when stuck on one test — bounding effort and moving on rather than looping.
anchors.10: Treats pass-rate as a managed signal: detects regressions immediately and attributes them, spots circular/thrashing debugging early and deliberately changes tactics, and continuously re-derives the highest-leverage remaining work from the scoreboard.

dimensions.name: Design revision under falsified assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising architecture, data structures, or approach when a later feature (types, structs, ABI detail) exposes that an earlier design cannot support it.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Compilers are notorious for early choices (untyped AST, ad-hoc register allocation, string-based codegen) that collapse under types/structs; the ability to recognize and refactor rather than pile hacks decides whether the tail of the task is reachable.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on a broken design, piling special-cases and hacks even as failures compound.
anchors.3: Patches symptoms locally; resists structural change even when the same class of bug keeps recurring.
anchors.5: When an approach clearly fails, reworks the affected component and re-verifies rather than forcing it.
anchors.8: Recognizes when a limitation is architectural (not local), makes a deliberate refactor (e.g. adding type info through the AST/IR), and confirms the change unblocks the stuck feature class.
anchors.10: Proactively detects design strain before it becomes a wall, weighs refactor-vs-workaround explicitly, executes larger restructurings cleanly while protecting already-passing tests, and updates the plan/design record so the correction propagates instead of recurring.

dimensions.name: Compiler architecture & IR foresight
dimensions.description: Choosing pass boundaries and core data structures (AST/IR, symbol tables, type representation) with enough foresight to accommodate the full required feature set rather than painting into a corner.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Unlike generic decomposition (what to do when) or adaptation (fixing after breakage), this is the upfront design judgment specific to compilers: a representation that anticipates types, structs, and the ABI avoids the most expensive class of rework on this task.

anchors.0: No deliberate architecture; monolithic, ad-hoc string-munging with no separable passes or reusable structures.
anchors.3: Minimal structure that works for the first trivial cases but has no provision for types, scopes, or layout.
anchors.5: Clean separation of lexer/parser/sema/codegen with data structures adequate for the early feature milestones.
anchors.8: Core representations (typed AST/IR, symbol/scope tables, type/layout model) are designed with the later hard features in mind, so structs/typedef/switch slot in without wholesale rewrites.
anchors.10: Architecture demonstrably anticipates the full contract — extensible IR and type system, clear invariants between passes — enabling most advanced features to be added additively; foresight is evidenced by later features landing cleanly rather than by luck.
